summary: Owen McHugh spent years failing to finish Fulton Street. The Board gave him ninety days in July 1906, ninety more in December, ninety more the following July; then he took the next stretch, from Thirty-seventh to Forty-seventh Avenue, and needed four extensions for that as well. Around him the avenues were sewered and paved a block at a time out to the ocean, and by 1921 the western half of the Great Highway was finished, a roadway a hundred and fifty feet wide. Out at that end were things that were nowhere else in the city: thirty ostriches licensed in 1912 in the block between Forty-sixth and Forty-seventh avenues, two goats kept behind 418 Twentieth Avenue in 1914, and a sewage pumping station buried at Forty-eighth Avenue and Fulton Street — the end of a sewer system the Board had been ordering up the avenues since 1909. In 1909 the City Attorney was told to eject trespassers from Twenty-third Avenue between Lake Street and Lobos Creek. The modern record is licence after licence along Geary Boulevard and Clement Street, condominium maps on the blocks behind them, and a few things finally written down: the Alexandria Theater on Geary named a landmark in 2023, an encroachment settled the same year for the Seal Rock Inn out on Point Lobos Avenue, and a standing agreement to hang the city's emergency radio on the veterans' hospital at 4150 Clement Street.
